payload.definition: A container image packages application code and its dependencies; the runtime executes it under the selected isolation model. options.explanation: The stated EKS managed-node mode requires customer upgrade action; do not infer Fargate or another service mode’s responsibilities.

records.title: Allocate a concrete cloud boundary
records.changeNote: Initial standalone C04 w5 AI-authored draft; no independent educator/legal approval or publication.
records.priorAttemptImpact: New draft ID; existing versions and attempts remain unchanged. Future attempts must retain this exact reference.

payload.prompt: Fictional Larch Dispatch uses ordinary Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL (not RDS Custom) and EKS on EC2 managed node groups. An image supplier supplies the application and base-image fixes but does not operate the cloud account. Allocate provider, customer and supplier actions for six controls: physical infrastructure; platform/node and application patching; identity/authorisation; network exposure; data/key/recovery protection; logging/incident response. Name internal accountable roles. Flag at least two service assumptions requiring provider confirmation, what evidence and owner will confirm each, and what changes if either is false. Distinguish supplier fix delivery from rollout.
payload.annotatedExample:
Physical infrastructure: AWS operates facilities/underlying hosts for both services; the customer cloud owner records the service scope. The image supplier has no facility role. Patching: AWS maintains the ordinary RDS platform; the database owner checks pending maintenance, engine support and application compatibility. For EKS, AWS manages the control plane and provides patched optimised node images; the platform owner upgrades the managed node group. The application owner deploys repaired application images for EKS; the supplier supplies those repairs and dependency information. A supplied fix is not a completed rollout. Identity: the customer identity and database/application owners approve database grants, AWS permissions and Kubernetes access; AWS operates the service mechanisms; the supplier receives no standing administrator access. Network: the customer network owner restricts RDS connections and EKS API/workload paths; AWS operates underlying networking. Data/key/recovery: the data and recovery owners choose access, supported encryption/key settings and recoverability targets and test restoration; AWS operates selected storage/backup functions. Logging/response: service teams enable and collect relevant logs, test alerts and own escalation; AWS handles its infrastructure incidents, and the supplier supports image-vulnerability investigation. For the last three rows the image supplier has no routine operational permission in the stated arrangement.

First confirm that this is ordinary RDS rather than RDS Custom and which engine/maintenance actions are available or mandatory: the database owner checks the exact service documentation and pending-maintenance evidence with AWS support if unclear. If the service is Custom, revise the OS/maintenance allocation before approving it. Second confirm EKS compute is EC2 managed node groups rather than Fargate or Auto Mode: the platform owner checks the deployed compute configuration against current EKS guidance. A different mode changes the infrastructure update handoff. Retain configuration snapshots and dated support clarification; the customer service owner remains accountable for the business consequence. Annotation: all six rows allocate activities for both workloads without claiming that the supplier operates the account or that one generic patching label is sufficient.

records.title: Review three supply-chain checks
records.changeNote: Initial standalone C04 w5 AI-authored draft; no independent educator/legal approval or publication.
records.priorAttemptImpact: New draft ID; existing versions and attempts remain unchanged. Future attempts must retain this exact reference.

payload.prompt: A fictional containerised appointment service has budget for three release checks. Propose exactly three checks that collectively cover source, dependency, build and deployment. State which stages each covers, its owner, evidence and what it fails to detect. For the highest anchors, trace approved inputs to the built and deployed digest; include allowed and rejected tests, explain signature and scan limits, and name an unresolved-risk decision owner and revisit trigger.
payload.annotatedExample:
Check 1 combines source and dependency review. The application lead requires a reviewed source commit, locked dependency versions and a component inventory assessed against known vulnerabilities and supplier notices. Retain review approvals, lockfile/inventory and the dated triage result. It can miss malicious business logic, unknown vulnerabilities and unrecorded components.

Check 2 assesses build integrity. The build-platform owner uses restricted, short-lived build credentials and an isolated build job, retaining the input commit, dependency inputs, build identity, output digest and verified signed provenance under an approved trust policy. This links the release to check 1. Test that the approved build produces acceptable verification evidence and an unapproved build identity fails verification. A compromised approved builder or signing key can still produce trusted-looking evidence; a signature is not a vulnerability assessment.

Check 3 enforces deployment policy. The platform owner admits only the reviewed digest with the expected trusted verification evidence and required nonprivileged configuration. In isolation, test the approved deployment succeeds and an unsigned/unapproved digest and unnecessary privileged manifest are denied. Retain admission decisions, deployed digest and test results. This cannot detect every application flaw, credential misuse or later runtime compromise. The service owner decides whether to defer release or accept bounded residual risk after the three evidence sets are compared. Revisit on a new critical dependency advisory, failed rejection test or signing-key concern. Annotation: the first combined check permits four-stage coverage with three checks; no single green result is treated as a safety guarantee.

payload.prompt: A supplier says: “Our signed container means the release is safe.” Write a brief executive response for a fictional delivery service. Explain the useful signature claim and its limits, request the exact digest, verification-policy result and relevant assessment evidence, and give a justified release/defer decision with a next evidence action, accountable role, residual risk and revisit condition. For the top anchors, weigh the cost of delay against exposure and state what this evidence and self-assessment cannot establish.
payload.annotatedExample:
A signature verified under our trusted policy supports a claim about the origin and integrity of this particular image. It does not establish that its dependencies or business logic are safe, or that the deployment grants only necessary privileges. Please supply the exact digest, trusted-signer verification result, build/input record, current component assessment and explanation of unresolved findings.

I would defer this fictional release until the application lead confirms the relevant component finding and the platform lead demonstrates that an unapproved digest and unnecessary privileged manifest are rejected. Delay postpones a dispatch improvement; releasing without those checks could expose order data or interrupt delivery. The service owner is accountable for that tradeoff and any time-limited exception. Even after checks, unknown vulnerabilities and compromise of an approved builder remain possible. Revisit at tomorrow’s release review, or earlier if a new advisory or verification failure appears. Annotation: the decision is conditional on missing evidence, not on an assertion that signatures are useless. This response and its rubric are self-assessed practice; neither signature evidence nor completion proves competence or future security.

records.title: Practical cloud responsibility and supply-chain review
records.changeNote: Initial standalone C04 w5 AI-authored draft; no independent educator/legal approval or publication.
records.priorAttemptImpact: New draft ID; existing versions and attempts remain unchanged. Future attempts must retain this exact reference.

payload.brief: Fictional Larch Dispatch plans ordinary RDS for PostgreSQL (not RDS Custom) and EKS with EC2 managed node groups. A supplier delivers application and base-image fixes, but has no cloud-account operations role. The COO wants evidence before authorising production. Use the six control areas from the lesson: physical infrastructure; platform/node/application patching; identity/authorisation; network exposure; data/key/recovery protection; logging/incident response.
payload.deliverable: Produce six responsibility rows covering both workloads with provider/customer/supplier actions, internal accountable roles and evidence. Flag at least two service/mode assumptions, confirming owner, provider evidence and changed action if false. Design exactly three checks spanning source, dependency, build and deployment with owner/evidence/limitation for each. For top anchors trace inputs to the deployed digest, test allowed/rejected deployments, explain signature/scan limits, compare delay/exposure, give a business decision, residual risk, safe stop/rollback condition and dated/event-triggered review. State self-assessment provenance and evidence limits.
constraints: Use only fictional facts and synthetic data in an isolated test plan; do not operate a real cloud account or submit employer evidence.
Keep the selected RDS/EKS modes explicit; if proposing a different mode, revise the allocation and cite its exact official boundary.
No paid course or external account is required. No legal, mastery, readiness or independent-review claim follows from completion.
payload.annotatedExample:
For both stated workloads, record six rows. (1) AWS operates facilities and underlying infrastructure; the customer cloud owner retains dated service-scope documentation. The image supplier has no facility role. (2) AWS maintains the RDS platform and EKS control plane, and supplies optimised node images; the customer database owner retains pending-maintenance and compatibility results, and the platform owner retains managed-node upgrade results. The supplier delivers repaired application/base-image components; the application owner retains deployment tests and the repaired running digest. (3) AWS supplies identity mechanisms; customer identity, database and platform owners approve access and retain role/grant exports plus allowed/denied tests. The supplier has no standing administrator access. (4) AWS operates underlying networking; the customer network owner configures and tests RDS, cluster-management and workload paths, retaining rules and connection-test results. (5) AWS operates selected storage/recovery functions; customer data/key/recovery owners retain access/key configuration and an isolated usable-restore result against their targets. The image supplier has no routine role in rows 4–5. (6) AWS handles infrastructure incidents; customer service teams retain configured-log and test-alert results and an escalation record. The supplier investigates image findings and delivers repairs. Confirm ordinary RDS versus Custom and EC2 managed node groups versus alternative EKS modes before approving the allocation. The database owner checks the exact RDS service and maintenance evidence, obtaining provider clarification if needed; Custom changes the OS-maintenance allocation. The platform owner checks deployed compute against current EKS guidance; a switch to Fargate changes node-infrastructure ownership. Revise the handoff before relying on either assumption if it is false.

For delivery, (1) the application lead reviews the approved commit and locked components, retaining approvals/inventory/dated triage; malicious logic and unknown flaws may escape. (2) The build owner restricts credentials and verifies build evidence tying those inputs to the output digest; retain build identity, inputs and verification result. A compromised approved builder can still sign harmful content. (3) The platform owner admits only that approved digest with verified trust evidence and limited privileges; retain deployment/admission results. Test an approved nonprivileged deployment succeeds, an unapproved digest and unnecessary privileged manifest fail. Application flaws and later credential misuse remain possible. A clean scan covers known detectable findings at that time, not all vulnerabilities.

Recommend a synthetic pre-release test before production approval. One day of delay postpones dispatch improvements; proceeding without proven rejection paths may expose order data and interrupt dispatch. The service owner is accountable for that tradeoff and time-limited exceptions. Stop if the test reaches production data or credentials. For a later authorised rollout, the platform owner retains the prior approved digest/configuration and a tested rollback path; stop or roll back when agreed business acceptance or denial checks fail. Revisit at tomorrow’s review, earlier on a critical advisory, failed rejection or key-trust concern. Annotation: this example covers each exercise criterion; another allocation or release decision needs equivalent service-specific evidence. It is self-reported fictional practice with rubric self-assessment, not independent educator review or proof of future security.

sections.heading: Begin with the service and the business consequence
sections.body: A cloud contract can remove hardware work while leaving an exposed database untouched. The leadership question is which activity is performed by whom, how its result is checked and who decides what to do when it fails. This lesson supports the weekly outcome: review shared responsibility and key AWS/Azure risks. You will allocate six controls across a managed database and a container workload, then propose three delivery checks covering four stages. All organisations and decisions here are fictional; these are technical governance examples, not legal obligations.

sections.heading: Define the boundary before assigning an owner
sections.body:
Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) supplies computing resources on which the customer manages operating systems and applications. EC2 and Azure Virtual Machines illustrate this boundary: the provider operates underlying infrastructure, while the customer manages the guest OS, software and selected network rules. Platform as a service (PaaS) moves more platform operation to the provider; software as a service (SaaS) supplies an application. These categories orient the discussion but do not replace the selected service’s documentation. “Managed” alone does not identify a patching, recovery or logging owner.

Separate the provider, the customer and an additional software or operations supplier. A supplier may repair an image or perform contracted operations. The customer still needs an internal accountable role to approve access, demand evidence and escalate failure. Responsibility here means an operational activity; it does not determine contractual liability. Write “platform team rolls out the patched node image” rather than “patching is shared.”

sections.heading: Containers introduce several distinct update boundaries
sections.body:
A container image packages application files and dependencies. A registry stores images; a runtime executes them; an orchestrator such as Kubernetes schedules workloads and manages their desired state. Its control plane exposes management functions, while worker nodes execute workloads. Ordinary Linux containers on a node share its kernel: an application-image rebuild does not replace that kernel. Privileged workloads or sensitive host mounts can expand the consequences of compromise. Alternative isolation technologies and managed modes require their own assessment.

A node machine image is the template used to start its operating system and associated software; it is different from an application container image. EKS manages its Kubernetes control plane. With EC2 managed node groups, AWS supplies updated optimised machine images and the customer upgrades the node groups. Fargate assumes additional infrastructure responsibilities. AKS also manages control-plane components; AKS Standard and Automatic differ in baseline configuration and operational ownership. Confirm the actual mode and node-update process. None of these labels transfers the customer’s application-image, data-access and workload-permission decisions wholesale.

sections.heading: Worked executive example 1 · Six controls for an AWS service
sections.body:
Larch Dispatch runs ordinary RDS for PostgreSQL, not RDS Custom, and its application on EKS EC2 managed node groups. An external image supplier provides application repairs without operating the account. The COO wants an explicit allocation before funding the migration.

1. Physical infrastructure: AWS operates facilities and underlying infrastructure for both services. The customer cloud owner verifies the selected services’ scope; the image supplier has no physical-control activity.
2. Patching: AWS operates RDS platform maintenance; the database owner checks engine support, pending actions and compatibility. AWS operates the EKS control plane and supplies optimised node images; the platform owner upgrades node groups. The supplier repairs application/base-image components; the application owner rebuilds, tests and deploys the approved image.
3. Identity and authorisation: AWS operates service mechanisms; the customer identity, database and platform owners approve permissions and test denied actions. The supplier has no standing administrator access.
4. Network exposure: AWS operates underlying networking; the customer network owner restricts database connections, cluster management and workload paths.
5. Data, keys and recovery: AWS operates selected storage and recovery mechanisms; customer data/key/recovery owners configure permitted access and supported protection, set targets and test usable recovery.
6. Logging and incident response: AWS handles its infrastructure incidents; customer service teams select and retain relevant logs, test alerts and lead their response. The supplier investigates image findings and provides repairs. It has no routine operational role in rows 4–5.

The database owner must confirm ordinary versus Custom service boundaries and engine-specific maintenance timing. The platform owner must confirm managed-node compute rather than Fargate or another mode. Retain configuration and official service evidence, seeking provider clarification where ambiguous. A changed answer changes the allocation. The COO funds database maintenance coordination and node rollout testing because a supplier-delivered fix alone does not keep dispatch available.

sections.heading: AWS and Azure risks follow the configured path
sections.body:
An overly broad AWS permission or Azure role can let a compromised account change data or controls. A reachable RDS endpoint or AKS management endpoint creates a network path; authentication and authorisation must still constrain actions. Network restriction alone does not prove application permission is correct. A vulnerable base image, exposed secret or unnecessary workload privilege can undermine a managed cluster. Enable the relevant diagnostic evidence, assign response ownership and test both allowed and denied actions. Provider infrastructure assurance does not establish that these customer settings are correct.

For Azure, check the selected AKS mode’s baseline and configured policy rather than assuming that every cluster has identical defaults. For either provider, identify key and identity dependencies before recovery testing. A backup feature and encrypted storage do not establish a usable restore or prevent an authorised plaintext export. These are service risks to investigate, not a claim that one provider is inherently safer.

sections.heading: Three checks can span four delivery stages
sections.body:
A software supply chain includes source code, dependencies, build systems and deployment. Dependencies include base images and libraries. A software bill of materials (SBOM) inventories components; it does not prove that the inventory is complete or that those components are safe. A digest identifies image content. A signature checked against a trusted signer supports integrity/origin under that policy. Provenance describes claimed build inputs and process. A compromised trusted builder or signer can still produce harmful content.

First combine source and dependency checks: require reviewed changes, locked inputs, component inventory and dated vulnerability triage. The application lead retains approvals and findings; unknown flaws or malicious logic may escape. Second check build integrity: restrict build access and credentials, record the approved inputs and output digest, and verify build evidence under a defined trust policy. The build owner retains those records; a compromised approved builder remains a limitation. Third enforce deployment policy: admit the approved digest with required verification and limited privileges. The platform owner retains admission and runtime-configuration evidence; this does not detect every application flaw or later credential misuse. Together the checks cover four stages without pretending three scans provide universal assurance.

sections.heading: Worked executive example 2 · A signed Azure release
sections.body:
A fictional appointments service uses AKS Standard. Its supplier presents a valid signature and requests a privileged deployment. The operations director asks for immediate release before the morning booking peak. The security lead requests the exact digest, trusted-signer policy result, input/build record and current component findings. The platform team tests that the approved nonprivileged deployment works and that an unapproved digest and unnecessary privileged manifest are denied.

The director defers this candidate until the excessive privilege is removed and the three check owners produce their evidence. The delay postpones an improvement, while the proposed privilege could widen an attacker’s access after compromise. The service owner records this tradeoff, residual unknown vulnerabilities and a review the next morning. A failed rejection test or signing-key concern triggers earlier review. A green signature was useful evidence of a narrower claim; it never justified the manifest’s permissions.

sections.heading: Practice · Make the handoffs and limits reviewable
sections.body:
Complete scenario-w5-cloud-review using the two specified workloads and six control rows. For each row distinguish provider/customer/supplier activities, internal accountable role and evidence. Identify at least two assumptions requiring provider confirmation, the confirming owner and what changes if false. Propose exactly three checks spanning source, dependency, build and deployment; each needs an owner, retained evidence and a limitation.

For the highest rubric anchors, explain supplier-fix/customer-rollout handoffs, trace approved inputs to the deployed digest, test allowed and rejected deployments, and reject signature/scan certainty. Compare delay with exposure; give an accountable business decision, residual risk, safe stop/rollback condition and dated or event-triggered review. Keep the exercise synthetic and isolated. Reading, resource use, legacy task completion, card recall, question attempts and applied self-assessment remain separate. No completion or score establishes mastery, certification readiness or independent review.

payload.workedExample: For ordinary RDS and EKS EC2 managed node groups, separate provider infrastructure/platform operation, customer configuration and rollout, and supplier image repairs. In an AKS Standard release, a valid image signature does not justify unnecessary workload privileges; the service owner bounds release with evidence and a revisit condition.
misconceptions: Managed means every patch, permission, backup and response is the provider’s responsibility.
An application-image rebuild patches the node kernel or every container service has the same ownership boundary.
A signed image, SBOM or clean vulnerability scan establishes that a release is safe.
